title: The Marketing Fund Trap: The Levy Franchisors Collect but Don't Actually Own
linkedin:
A franchise invoice looks like one number. It isn't.

Royalty income and marketing fund contributions land in the same transfer, on the same day, from the same franchisee. One is the franchisor's own income. The other is collected for a specific purpose, and most franchise agreements are clear it can only be spent on marketing that benefits the network, not on general working capital.

The two numbers blend quietly. A quiet month gets covered by what looks like spare cash sitting in the account. Repeat that often enough and the marketing fund balance and the actual bank balance drift apart without anyone noticing exactly when.

October is when this surfaces. Franchise marketing calendars peak in the run-up to Christmas trading, and campaigns need to be booked and paid well before December. If the fund has already been drawn down for general cash flow, the shortfall lands at the exact moment franchisees are watching most closely, comparing what they paid in against what they can see being spent on their behalf.

Under the Franchising Code of Conduct, franchisors must report annually on how the fund was spent. That obligation exists because the money is held for the network's benefit, not as discretionary income. Treating it as a once-a-year compliance task, rather than a number reconcilable at any point, is usually what leaves a franchisor scrambling in November to explain a shortfall they did not see coming.

The fix is simple to describe and easy to neglect: keep the fund on its own ledger, reviewed with the same quarterly discipline as the rest of the business.

A pattern we see often with franchise systems across Brisbane, Queensland, New South Wales and Victoria: royalty income and marketing fund contributions arrive in the same bank transfer, but only one of them actually belongs to the franchisor.

The marketing fund is collected for a specific purpose, usually national campaigns and brand assets, and most franchise agreements are clear it shouldn't be spent on general running costs. The mix-up tends to happen quietly, a slow month covered by what looks like spare cash, repeated often enough that the fund balance and the real bank balance drift apart.

October is when this becomes obvious. Franchise marketing calendars peak in the lead-up to Christmas trading, and campaigns need to be booked and paid well before December. A fund that has quietly run thin over the year is a much harder conversation with franchisees in November than it would have been to prevent earlier.
